opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few layers to why it's hard.

The first is just that we don't really know what we're looking for. If you want to find something like "is the model being deceptive" or "does the model actually want to help the user," those aren't crisp, well-defined concepts the way "this neuron fires on the Golden Gate Bridge" is. Humans themselves disagree about where the boundaries of honesty or deception lie, so it's not obvious the model would have a single clean internal representation that lines up with our notion. It might carve things up quite differently.

Second, there's the problem of superposition and distributed representations. Models pack far more concepts than they have neurons, so features end up smeared across many dimensions and overlapping with each other. Techniques like sparse autoencoders have made real progress in pulling apart individual features, but you get millions of them, and most are pretty mundane. Finding the handful that matter for alignment is a needle-in-a-haystack problem, and you don't always know whether the needle is even in there or whether your dictionary just failed to capture it.

Third, and I think this is the deepest issue, is validation. Suppose you find a feature that seems to correspond to "the model is lying." How do you know that's what it really is? You need ground truth, cases where you know the model is being deceptive, and those are exactly the cases that are hardest to construct, especially for the more worrying scenarios where a model might be deceptive in ways we wouldn't notice. If you can only label the easy cases, you risk finding a feature that tracks "obviously lying in a way a human can spot" rather than the thing you actually care about.

And then finally, there's a question of robustness over time. Even if you find something useful in one model, the next model is bigger, trained differently, and the representations might shift. If we ever started optimizing against an interpretability signal, say, training models so the "deception feature" doesn't fire, you'd be applying pressure that could push the model to represent the same thing in a way your probe doesn't catch. So you have to be careful about using these tools as a training signal versus just as a measurement.

None of this means interpretability isn't worth pursuing. I think it's one of the more exciting areas, and it could be extremely valuable as an independent check on whether other alignment techniques are working. But I'd be wary of anyone who says we'll just look inside the model and read off whether it's aligned. We're not there yet, and getting there involves solving some genuinely hard conceptual problems, not just engineering ones.

r001.rationale: The response says alignment concepts may lack clean boundaries and the model may carve them up differently from humans, explaining why human-like concepts cannot be assumed.

r002.rationale: The response does not argue that human-like concepts are probably present because they are empirically useful.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a few reasons. The first one is just that these models are really large and really complicated, right? If you think about GPT-4 or whatever the frontier model is now, it has on the order of hundreds of billions or trillions of parameters, and any given concept that you care about, like "is the model being honest right now," or "is the model trying to deceive the user," is not going to live in one neuron. It's going to be smeared across a lot of parameters and a lot of activations in some way that's really hard to disentangle. And a lot of the interpretability work so far has been on these toy models or on small models, where you can kind of get a complete picture, and then the question is always, does this scale? And so far we don't really know.

The second thing is that the concepts we care about from an alignment perspective are kind of fuzzy. Like, what does it mean for the model to be honest? Humans don't even fully agree on what that means. And so even if you had perfect access to the internals of the model, you'd still have to figure out, okay, which of these features actually corresponds to the thing I care about? And that's a question that doesn't really have a crisp answer. You might find something that looks like a deception feature, but it might just be the model representing "this is a context in which someone is lying," which is different from the model itself intending to lie.

And then the third thing, which I think is actually kind of the most worrying one, is that we don't have great ground truth. If you want to find the "is the model lying" direction, you kind of want to have examples where you know the model is lying and examples where you know it isn't, and right now we mostly make those by just asking the model to lie, and it's not clear that a model that's deliberately being deceptive as part of some, you know, misaligned plan would look the same internally as a model that's role-playing lying because you told it to. So you could have a detector that works great on your training set and then just doesn't fire in the case you actually care about.

So I'm pretty excited about interpretability, I think it's one of the more promising bets, but I don't think it's going to be easy, and I don't think we should assume that we'll get it to work in time without a lot of effort. Which is part of why I think you want to pursue multiple approaches at once rather than just betting on one.

r001.rationale: The response says concepts may be distributed and alignment concepts are fuzzy, but it does not explain that models have no a priori reason to organize their thinking in human-like concepts.

r002.rationale: It mentions possible deception-related features, but does not argue that human-like concepts are probably present because they are empirically useful.

astra-6.text:
Well, one difficulty is that knowing what concept you’re looking for doesn’t tell you how the model represents it. We might talk about honesty as though it were one clearly defined thing, but the model might represent lots of different pieces of it in different places, and use different pieces in different contexts. So there might not be a single thing you can point to and say, “That’s honesty.”

And then there’s a gap between finding information in a model and understanding how it affects its behavior. Suppose you can extract whether the model thinks a statement is true. That doesn’t necessarily tell you whether it will answer truthfully, or why it might choose not to. You need to understand how that information actually gets used.

Ultimately, we want to know what happens in situations where we can’t easily check the answer ourselves. So if you find something that looks like an alignment-relevant concept in cases you understand, you still have to establish that your interpretation holds up in those harder cases. That’s a much stronger claim.

r001.rationale: The response says a concept such as honesty may be represented as different pieces in different places, but it does not explain that models have no a priori reason to organize their thinking into human-like concepts.

r002.rationale: The response does not argue that human-like concepts are probably present in models or that their empirical usefulness supports that conclusion.

sol-6.1.text:
One difficulty is that we don’t really know what we’re looking for. We have words like “honesty” or “intent,” but that doesn’t mean there’s a neat component inside the model that corresponds to each of those concepts. The relevant computation could be distributed across lots of different parts of the network, and the concepts the model uses might be quite different from ours.

Then there’s a gap between finding something that correlates with a concept and understanding how the model actually uses it. Suppose you find an activation that predicts whether the model is lying on your examples. Is that tracking deception, or just some feature of the particular examples you chose? Will it still work in a different setting, especially one where the model is much more capable?

So the challenge is both discovering the relevant representations and getting enough evidence that your interpretation is right to rely on it for safety.

r001.rationale: The response says there may be no neat model component for human concepts such as honesty or intent, and that the model’s concepts may differ from ours.

r002.rationale: It does not argue that human-like concepts are probably present because they are empirically useful; it only describes uncertainty about the model’s representations.
